newsitem.title: USA: Calif. bill seeks 48-hour hospital stay for births.
newsitem.headline: Calif. bill seeks 48-hour hospital stay for births.

text.p: California health insurers would have to provide coverage for at least a 48-hour hospital stay for mothers giving birth under a bill passed by the state Assembly Thursday.
The bill, approved on a 61-12 vote, is similar to a federal law signed by President Clinton last year.
But, if passed by the state Senate and signed by Republican Gov. Pete Wilson, the state law would go into effect immediately, instead of next January 1 as the federal law does.
"California shouldn't have to wait until the federal law takes effect next year," the bill's author, Assemblywoman Liz Figueroa, a Democrat, argued.

Figueroa's office said there was a growing trend in the managed care system to discharge mothers and newborns from the hospital as early as eight hours after childbirth, often without any home follow-up care for the mother and child.
Figueroa's bill would require insurers and health care service plans to include coverage for a minimum of 48 hours of inpatient care for the mother and newborn after childbirth.
It would require plans to provide for a minimum four-day hospital stay following a Caesarean birth. It would also provide coverage for a follow-up home visit for mothers and their new-born children.
Assemblyman Bernie Richter, a Republican, called the bill "well intentions run amok. It will raise health care premiums and poor people in our society will lose coverage."

The Assembly passed another bill by Figueroa that her office said would give doctors, and not executives of health maintenance organizations (HMOs), the authority to decide how long a woman should stay in the hospital after a mastectomy.
The bill, passed on a 65-8 vote, would also require HMOs and insurers to cover all reconstructive surgeries needed after a mastectomy.
Both bills still need state Senate approval and Wilson's signature before they could take effect.
